title: Special Report, My So-Called Alpha School
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Riley reconstructs the first weeks of Alpha School's high school boot camp from what students themselves posted on social media, organising the piece into reporting, the school's response, outside reactions and his own commentary. He is careful about provenance, explaining that he and colleagues initially assumed the accounts were a prank, that many posts appear to be AI generated, and that he investigated independently before concluding they are genuine. He also lays out the only two possibilities he can see: either the accounts are effectively Potemkin students steered by employees as a public relations campaign, or they are authentic and accurately describe the programme. The practices he documents include heart-rate monitoring while students watch recordings of their parents criticising them, required audience building on X, and initiation activities students say were never advertised. His sharpest objection is a claim about labelling rather than technology, since Alpha markets itself under the banner of the science of learning, a term he helped popularise, while running extreme behaviourist rituals alongside unguided internet discovery. He treats students throughout as blameless, and gives particular weight to one who messaged the founder to say the exercises clashed with deeper values.
points: Builds the account from students' own public posts while blurring names and avatars, and states plainly that the students are not the target of the critique.
Frames the evidentiary problem honestly, since many posts appear AI generated, and narrows it to two readings: a staged campaign using student avatars, or an authentic picture of the programme.
Documents biometric monitoring in which students watch recorded parental criticism while their heart rate is checked against a baseline.
Argues the school appropriates the science of learning label while practising extreme behaviourism and unguided internet discovery at the same time.
Notes that students reported surprise at initiation activities the school does not advertise, and connects the pattern to research on shame and stigma rituals in selective groups.
quotes: It’s a report on life in the first weeks of high school at Alpha School, based on what students are sharing on social media.

However, after conducting an independent investigation, I believe that the accounts are legitimate, and that taken as a whole, the tweets convey aspects of student life in the first weeks of Alpha School’s high school, the period called “boot camp.

Please note further, while I have many critiques aimed at Alpha School’s leadership and the vision of education they are promoting, the students are blameless, they are simply teenagers trying to make their way in the world.

When I shared screenshots with my friends in education about Alpha School biometrically monitoring their students, their first reaction was typically “WHAT?” or “WTF,” soon followed by “this can’t be real” or “this is The Onion, right?

It’s possible that Alpha School has created de facto “Potemkin students,” meaning that, while the accounts may be affiliated with actual students, the tweets are largely being directed or steered by Alpha School employees. A PR campaign using student avatars, essentially.

And then on top of this we have Alpha School cloaking itself under the banner of “the science of learning,” a term I helped popularize, while promoting radically extreme behaviorist practices such as heart-rate monitoring (!) and pure unadulterated discovery learning by combing the Internet (!!!)
This is madness. Actually, my 10-year-old daughter said it best after hearing these boot-camp activities described to her: That’s not okay.

Numerous students expressed complete surprise by this activity — and indeed, boot camp itself — and as far as I can tell, nowhere does Alpha School publicly advertise such activities are part of its program. I find that telling.
